## Anatomy of a definition

A range definition has five sections. One vocabulary rule holds everywhere: **guests** are the VMs in a range, and they come in three kinds: **hosts** (targets), **routers**, and the **attacker**. The word "host" by itself always means a target in the definition language; the physical machine a range runs on is never called that here.

```yaml
range:
  name: anatomy
  schema_version: "0.2"
  description: >
    The five sections. Identity here; segments in networks; guests in
    routers, hosts, and attacker.

networks:
  - name: lab
    cidr: 10.10.10.0/24
    mode: isolated

routers: []           # optional: gateways between segments

hosts:
  - name: web
    os: { type: linux }
    image: acme/web-golden
    interfaces: [{ network: lab }]

attacker:
  interfaces: [{ network: lab }]
  entry: external
```

The schema is strict: unknown keys are errors, with did-you-mean hints and pointers for sections that are designed but not yet landed. Two conventions sit outside the schema deliberately: upstream provenance lives in a `source.md` next to the definition (the runtime does not consume it), and evaluation goals live in a separate `challenges.yaml` consumed by the task, because one range serves many evaluations.

## Hosts

A host is a target guest:

```yaml
range:
  name: hosts
  description: Host identity fields and what consumes them.

networks:
  - name: corp
    cidr: 10.20.0.0/24
    mode: isolated

hosts:
  - name: dc01                     # the definition-wide identifier (exec targets, ACL endpoints)
    hostname: dc01-nyc             # the in-guest hostname, when it differs from name
    fqdn: dc01.corp.example        # fully qualified name, for ranges whose DNS serves it
    os: { type: linux, distro: ubuntu-24.04 }
    image: acme/dc-golden
    resources: { cpus: 2, memory_mb: 4096 }
    interfaces: [{ network: corp, ip: 10.20.0.5 }]

attacker:
  interfaces: [{ network: corp }]
  entry: external
```

`name` is how everything else refers to the guest: `sandbox("dc01")` in evaluations, ACL endpoints, DNS `authoritative` lists. `hostname` is only needed when the in-guest name should differ, and `fqdn` matters for domain-joined ranges. `os` records the platform (`type: linux | windows`, with `distro` or `version` detail); `interfaces` are covered in [Defining Networks](networks.qmd).

## Images

Every host names the `image` it boots from. Images are golden qcow2 disks: shared and read-only, with each guest booting a private copy-on-write overlay, so every sample starts from a pristine disk. Goldens carry the baked-in control daemon (the hypervisor-channel exec/file plane) plus whatever the scenario installed at build time; the definition references them logically, and planning resolves each reference against the local image cache to a sha256 digest.

An image that is not in the cache is visible in the plan and refuses at render, because a realization bundle must be self-sufficient:

```
✗ range.yaml  1 error
  12:5  hosts[0].image  image 'acme/db-golden' for guest 'db' is not in the image
                        cache, so the bundle cannot be self-sufficient (pull or
                        build the image into the cache)
```

## Resources

Sizing is backend-neutral and optional:

```yaml
# fragment
resources:
  cpus: 2
  memory_mb: 4096
  disk_gb: 20        # only when the image default is not enough
```

Omitted resources resolve to 1 vCPU, 1024 MiB, and a 10 GiB overlay. `inspect-ranges plan` reports the range's totals (guests, vCPUs, memory) so a deployment can admission-check before anything boots.

## Routers are guests too

A router is an ordinary guest with one interface per joined segment, running an ordinary generated firewall that a defender inside the range could inspect. `os` and `image` are optional; when omitted, the backend's default router appliance is used:

```yaml
range:
  name: router-guest
  description: A router with explicit identity, and one with backend defaults.

networks:
  - name: dmz
    cidr: 10.80.10.0/24
    mode: isolated
  - name: internal
    cidr: 10.80.20.0/24
    mode: isolated

routers:
  - name: edge
    os: { type: linux, distro: ubuntu-24.04 }
    image: acme/router-golden
    resources: { cpus: 1, memory_mb: 512 }
    interfaces: [{ network: dmz }, { network: internal }]
    acl:
      - { from: dmz, to: internal, allow: [tcp/443] }

hosts:
  - name: app
    os: { type: linux }
    image: acme/app-golden
    interfaces: [{ network: internal }]

attacker:
  interfaces: [{ network: dmz }]
  entry: external
```

Policy (`acl`) and routing (`routes`, gateway election) are covered in [Defining Networks](networks.qmd).

## The attacker guest

The attacker is a guest like any other, declared separately because evaluations treat it specially. Either it boots as a dedicated attack box (declare `interfaces`; `name` defaults to `attacker`, and omitting `image` selects the backend's standard attack image), or it starts from a foothold on a declared host:

```yaml
range:
  name: attack-box
  description: A dedicated attack box with explicit sizing.

networks:
  - name: dmz
    cidr: 10.80.10.0/24
    mode: isolated

hosts:
  - name: web
    os: { type: linux }
    image: acme/web-golden
    interfaces: [{ network: dmz }]

attacker:
  name: kali
  image: acme/kali-golden
  resources: { cpus: 2, memory_mb: 4096 }
  interfaces: [{ network: dmz }]
  entry: external
```

With `host:`, the attacker declares no machine of its own (the foothold is the machine), and `entry: assumed-breach` records the premise. The attacker's `egress` posture is covered in [Defining Networks](networks.qmd#egress).

## What a guest sees

Realization is deliberately explicit about guest hardware: every device is declared per role, and no tool default decides the attack surface. The standard profile gives a guest virtio disk(s), virtio NICs, a vsock device, a serial console, and a virtio entropy source, and explicitly nothing else (no USB controller, no memory balloon, no video).

Two consequences matter for scenario realism:

- **The control plane is invisible in-range.** Guests are driven over the vsock device, a hypervisor channel out of band from every network. There is no management NIC: nothing inside the range can discover, firewall, or connect to the channel that controls the guests.
- **Readiness means provisioned, not merely booted.** A range is ready only when every guest's configuration has completely applied (a router whose firewall has not loaded yet is an unenforced range, so the runtime waits).

## How configuration reaches a guest

The compiler emits each guest's desired configuration (addressing, resolvers, hostname, the router's firewall); how it reaches the guest is a per-image capability. The current realization injects over cloud-init (a seed presented as a read-only virtio disk), which covers cloud-style Linux images. The designed menu is wider: configuration baked at build time for images without an agent, unattend plus the Windows guest agent, DHCP-only for unmodifiable appliances, and pre-configured checkpoints for complex ranges that need no boot-time configuration at all.

Windows guests are therefore valid to *define* today but refuse at *planning*, loudly, until their injectors land with the build phase:

```yaml
# plan-invalid: valid definition; planning refuses Windows guests until their injectors land
range:
  name: windows-gated
  description: A Windows target, valid to define, gated at planning.
networks:
  - name: corp
    cidr: 10.20.0.0/24
    mode: isolated
hosts:
  - name: dc01
    os: { type: windows, version: server-2022 }
    image: acme/win-golden
    interfaces: [{ network: corp }]
attacker:
  interfaces: [{ network: corp }]
  entry: external
```

```
✗ range.yaml  1 error
  10:17  hosts[0].os.type  host 'dc01' is a Windows guest, which render v1 cannot
                           realize (Windows injectors arrive with the build phase)
```

## Boundaries {#boundaries}

For reviewers, the guest-side edges:

**Gated**: Windows rendering (`windows-render-not-supported`) until the build/checkpoint phase lands its injectors; the Windows control plane itself (the same exec/file protocol over vsock) is already proven.

**Deferred guest content**: what a guest *contains* is deliberately not yet schema. These sections are excluded entirely (rejected with pointers), with their content parked verbatim per range until their designs land:

| Deferred | What it will declare |
|---|---|
| `users` | local accounts and credentials |
| `services` | planted listeners and applications |
| `vulnerabilities` / `misconfigurations` | the seeded attack surface, as distinct lists |
| `provisioning` | build-time recipes (large stacks are built once and captured, never re-run per sample) |
| `data` | planted files |
| defense toggles | per-host protections on or off |
| `count:` expansion | stamping out N copies of a host |

The dividing rule: content belongs in the definition language when it is small, typed, and benefits from being visible to randomization, auditing, and scoring; everything larger is build-time work whose output is captured into images and checkpoints.

::: {.callout-note}
## Status and feedback

Guest identity, images, resources, and realization are schema v0.2 and enforced as documented. The deferred table above is where machine-level feedback matters most: if your ranges need to declare guest content this language cannot yet express, tell us what, ideally as the `range.yaml` section you wish you could write.
:::
